metadata.setting: An imagined neighborhood clubhouse in El Segundo
metadata.scope_note: Three original concepts for an unspecified, imagined setting. No real site, commission, construction proposal, or architect endorsement is claimed.
metadata.modularity_note: Five named parts form a shared design vocabulary. Rearranging or replacing one part changes the proposed experience while keeping the rest of the concept available.
metadata.authorship_note: The concepts and interpretations are original editorial proposals for The Loom Broadcaster. Referenced projects retain their original authorship.
metadata.broadcast_status: All four segments are unpublished drafts.

part_types.name: Activity
part_types.description: What gives someone a reason to return?

concepts.name: Sunroom
concepts.pitch: A neighborhood living room where you can arrive alone, open a book, and join a conversation when you feel like it.

parts.name: Open canopy
parts.description: A common cover gathers the chairs and book table into one recognizable room.

parts.name: Reading chairs
parts.description: Separate seats form small pairs; some face the table and others face outward.

parts.name: Refill point
parts.description: A water stop at the edge invites a pause without needing to join the room.

parts.name: Book table
parts.description: A common surface welcomes open books, a notebook, or a conversation.

parts.name: Swap shelf
parts.description: A shelf invites people to leave a book and a handwritten recommendation.

tradeoffs: Small conversations take priority over big gatherings.
Quiet corners make the shared activity less visible.
A book exchange needs someone to keep it inviting.
concepts.rearrange_benefit: Turn the same chairs toward the table for a reading circle, then separate them again for quiet use.
concepts.replace_benefit: Replace the swap shelf with a neighborhood listening board while retaining the other four parts.

concepts.name: Long Table
concepts.pitch: A clubhouse organized around the easiest invitation in the neighborhood: pull up a seat and bring something to the table.

parts.name: Table canopy
parts.description: Shade follows the table, making the collective surface the focus.

parts.name: Pull-up seats
parts.description: Loose seats gather along the table or move aside for people to stand and work.

parts.name: Water corner
parts.description: A water stop off the main approach gives pausing its own place.

parts.name: Common table
parts.description: One common surface proposes different moments for meals, making, and conversation.

parts.name: Repair cart
parts.description: A separate cart proposes a bring-and-mend session, then leaves the table free.

tradeoffs: A central table makes social interaction hard to avoid.
Messy projects and meals compete for the same surface.
Shared use needs someone to reset the table.
concepts.rearrange_benefit: Move the seats and repair cart around the same table to shift the proposed scene from a shared meal to a making session.
concepts.replace_benefit: Swap the repair cart for a seed exchange or drawing station while keeping the gathering arrangement.

concepts.name: Play Yard
concepts.pitch: An open middle becomes the clubhouse, with the next game giving neighbors a reason to meet again.

parts.name: Sideline canopy
parts.description: Shade marks a place to watch and pause beside the proposed play area.

parts.name: Spectator seats
parts.description: Seats face the open middle and can turn into a circle when the game ends.

parts.name: Pause point
parts.description: A water stop beside the watching area makes a visible place to take a break.

parts.name: Game table
parts.description: A table holds scorecards, game pieces, and conversations between rounds.

parts.name: Chalk game
parts.description: Changeable ground marks invite participants to propose the next game.

tradeoffs: The open middle gives play priority over long conversations.
Watching the action leaves fewer private corners.
A shared game needs agreed rules and a way to pause.
concepts.rearrange_benefit: Turn the spectator seats toward one another and bring the game table closer for a quieter gathering using the same parts.
concepts.replace_benefit: Replace the chalk game with a story circle or neighborhood quiz while retaining the four supporting parts.

references.title: Kampung Admiralty
references.creator: WOHA
references.source_fact: WOHA describes a layered complex bringing a community plaza, medical centre, rooftop community park, and apartments for seniors together. Its project account emphasizes the benefits of locating different everyday uses close to one another.
references.our_interpretation: Ask how the five parts support one another. A water stop, table, and place to sit can be considered together instead of as five isolated objects.

references.title: Serpentine Pavilion 2021 and its Fragments
references.creator: Sumayya Vally, Counterspace
references.source_fact: Serpentine describes a pavilion informed by London's community gathering places, with four Fragments placed at partner organizations. Its Fragments account says the Valence Library piece could be used together or separated into smaller sections for recordings by Becontree Broadcasting.
references.our_interpretation: A place can have a life beyond one arrangement. Let a part change role or travel, while keeping the people and activities it serves visible in the story.

broadcasts.label: Discovery
broadcasts.text: The Traveling Trapper opens in an imagined El Segundo clubhouse. Five parts: shade, seating, water, a shared table, an activity. First, two real references: WOHA's Kampung Admiralty and Counterspace's 2021 Serpentine Pavilion.

broadcasts.label: Design
broadcasts.text: Same five parts, three proposed clubhouses: Sunroom for a quiet pause, Long Table for making together, Play Yard for the next game. Which kind of invitation would bring you back? These are speculative designs, with no real site selected.

broadcasts.label: Experiment
broadcasts.text: Try one change: turn the seats, move the table, or replace the activity. What changes about the invitation? The Traveling Trapper treats the clubhouse as five editable parts. This is a design exercise; no built performance has been tested.

broadcasts.label: Audience choice
broadcasts.text: Choose the next page of the Traveling Trapper: Sunroom, Long Table, or Play Yard. Then name one part you would rearrange or replace—and who that change would welcome. Your proposal can become the next design question.

rounds.name: Daylight
rounds.prompt: What makes you want to stay?
rounds.brief: Start with the everyday: a place to pause, a shared surface, a reason to return. Move one part and notice who the new arrangement invites.

part_prompts.shade: Where would you pause out of the sun?
part_prompts.seating: Which seats welcome a conversation, and which leave room to be alone?
part_prompts.water: Where does a quick refill become a friendly pause?
part_prompts.table: What can two strangers do at the same table?
part_prompts.activity: What could someone join for five minutes?

checklist: Can someone feel welcome arriving alone?
Is there a choice between company and quiet?
What invites people to use the shared table?
Is the refill point easy to find?

rounds.name: Night Market
rounds.prompt: What makes someone stop, watch, and join in?
rounds.brief: Set one shared table at the heart of a small evening market. Let a repair or demonstration draw people close, keep the way in easy to read, and leave room to sit back or refill.

part_prompts.shade: Where does the canopy frame a warmly lit welcome?
part_prompts.seating: Where can someone watch from a quieter edge before joining in?
part_prompts.water: Can a newcomer spot the refill point without crossing the activity?
part_prompts.table: What can people share, fix, or demonstrate around this table?
part_prompts.activity: What small demonstration starts a conversation without taking over the whole place?

checklist: Can a first-time visitor find the way in?
What invites them to join the shared table?
Can they find a quieter place to sit?
Is the refill point easy to spot?
